description: Car Hacking Village focuses on automotive cybersecurity, vehicle network architectures, Controller Area Network (CAN) security, and heavy vehicle protocols. Talks examine CAN bus bit-level manipulation, hardware tooling, and legacy vehicle communication standards.

talks.title: CAN Be Super Secure: Bit Smashing FTW
talks.teaser: Explores bit-level manipulation, error frame exploitation, and defensive hardening on Controller Area Networks.
talks.summary:
In this technical hardware presentation from the DEF CON Safe Mode Car Hacking Village, researcher Brent explores physical-layer defense mechanisms for Controller Area Network (CAN) bus architectures. Opening at 00:01, Brent reviews the inherent vulnerabilities of legacy broadcast CAN protocols, which lack message encryption, source authentication, and replay protection.

At 05:00, the presentation examines how unauthorized message injection and spoofed arbitration IDs allow attackers to manipulate critical vehicle ECUs. At 10:01, Brent introduces "bit smashing"—an active physical defense strategy where monitoring hardware actively injects dominant error bits onto the differential bus whenever rogue or spoofed frames are detected.

At 15:00 and 20:00, Brent demonstrates how bit smashing forces compromised ECUs into a "fail-silent" bus-off state, isolating malicious nodes and neutralizing denial-of-service and spoofing attacks in real time without requiring heavy cryptographic overhead. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Before J1939
talks.teaser: Examines the history, protocols, and diagnostic standards that preceded SAE J1939 in heavy-duty commercial vehicle networks.
talks.summary:
Researchers Dan Salloum and Thomas Hayes explore heavy commercial vehicle network security in the Car Hacking Village, investigating legacy communications protocols predating the widespread adoption of SAE J1939 [00:02, 00:07]. The presentation focuses on the SAE J1708 physical layer and its accompanying SAE J1587 application standard, which communicate over differential RS-485 serial buses [05:12, 05:22].

The researchers analyze the interaction between commercial tractors and semi-trailers, revealing how unencrypted telemetry—including odometer rotations, wheel speeds, tractor-trailer pairing IDs, and driver dispatch logs—transits the physical bus without cryptographic integrity checks [09:53]. They demonstrate custom Python-based hardware tooling developed to passively decode bus traffic and actively inject parameter identification (PID) messages [15:00, 20:19], illustrating how legacy industrial protocols leave commercial fleets vulnerable to tampering and spoofing [25:26].

talks.title: All Aboard the CAN Bus or Motorcycle
talks.teaser: Derrick shares a journey reverse engineering modern motorcycle CAN bus telemetry using custom microcontrollers, pulse-width modulation, and Python to construct an aftermarket digital gauge cluster.
talks.summary:
Motorcycle Electronics and CAN Bus Networks

Modern motorcycles increasingly implement Controller Area Network (CAN) architectures to coordinate engine control modules, ABS sensors, electronic throttles, and dashboard instrument clusters.

Building Custom Hardware and Simulation Fixtures

Derrick presents the hardware tooling required to tap into motorcycle wiring harnesses, combining low-cost microcontrollers, potentiometers, and pulse-width modulation (PWM) circuits to simulate engine RPM and speed signals.

Reverse Engineering CAN Bus Telemetry

The speaker details capturing, filtering, and deciphering proprietary motorcycle CAN packet frames in Python, identifying arbitration IDs and byte offsets for critical sensor telemetry.

Developing an Aftermarket Digital Gauge Cluster

The presentation demonstrates integrating the reversed telemetry stream into custom firmware driving an aftermarket instrument display, showing practical automotive hardware prototyping.
